Title: The Microstructure of AI Diffusion: Evidence from Firms, Business Functions, and Worker Tasks
Data Readiness Checklist
AI and Open Government Data Assets Request for Information (RFI)
Summary: In April 2024, the U.S. Department of Commerce issued a Request for Information (RFI) seeking public input on how to develop AI‑ready open government data assets and associated data dissemination standards to better support data‑driven AI, including generative AI.  The RFI frames Commerce’s long‑term publishing mission and asks for ways to improve the creation, curation, and distribution of its data so that AI systems can reliably use it.  The notice explicitly links AI‑readiness to the OPEN Government Data Act definition of “machine‑readable” (44 U.S.C. § 3502(18)), underscoring the need for data that can be processed by computers without human intervention while preserving semantic meaning.  Overall, Commerce positions the RFI as a step toward making federal data both machine‑readable and machine‑understandable, with the goal of enabling trustworthy AI use across public datasets.

Title: Comments on AI and Open Government Data Assets Request for Information
AI-Ready Federal Statistical Data: An Extension of Communicating Data Quality
Summary: This paper outlines how the Federal statistical community can make public data machine‑understandable so generative AI systems and large language models (LLMs) return accurate, trustworthy answers grounded in official statistics. It recommends the extension of the FCSM Framework for Data Quality—across Utility, Objectivity, and Integrity—to AI contexts by enriching statistical APIs with comprehensive, variable‑level metadata and standard schemas (e.g., DCAT, SDMX). The authors emphasize moving beyond “machine‑readable” to “machine‑understandable” data, aligning with open‑data requirements and dissemination directives, so AI can both find and correctly use authoritative statistics. They propose a practical roadmap of structured experiments: (1) baseline assessments of current AI responses and their sources/accuracy, (2) targeted API and metadata enhancements (including AI‑optimized structures and Model Context Protocols), and (3) cross‑agency learning to produce a reusable toolkit. The envisioned impact is improved AI accuracy, prioritization of authoritative federal data over nonauthoritative sources, and repeatable methods to benchmark AI readiness. Overall, the work is a call for coordinated standards, testing, and governance to ensure official statistics are reliably mediated by AI.

Title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Open Data: Guidelines and Best Practices
Summary: This Department of Commerce guidance defines what it means for public data to be AI‑ready—not merely machine‑readable but machine‑understandable—and provides actionable recommendations so generative AI systems can retrieve, interpret, and prioritize authoritative open data.  It frames Commerce’s goals as (1) improving the accuracy of AI responses that rely on Commerce data and (2) ensuring authoritative sources are prioritized over non‑authoritative ones.  The document maps how open data are used across the AI lifecycle (training, fine‑tuning, testing/validation, and retrieval/RAG) and organizes best practices into five areas: documentation; data/metadata formats; storage & dissemination; licensing & usage; and data quality & integrity.  Key technical recommendations include persistent identifiers and version control; comprehensive dataset‑ and variable‑level metadata aligned to DCAT‑3, Schema.org, and Croissant; publication in open, machine‑readable formats (e.g., CSV/JSON/JSON‑LD), with avoidance of PDFs for data/metadata; and provision of RESTful APIs with OpenAPI descriptions.  It also emphasizes rights/permissions clarity (robots.txt, data licenses vs. copyright licenses), automated data‑quality checks, and priming APIs for low‑latency retrieval to support RAG.  Future work points to digital signatures, AI‑readiness metrics, expanded education, cross‑agency partnerships (e.g., NAIRR), and standardized user feedback channels.  Overall, the paper is a living standard intended to be iteratively updated as technologies and user needs evolve.

Title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Open Data: Guidelines and Best Practices
Summary: This presentation outlines emerging challenges and best practices for preparing federal open data for effective use in generative AI systems, emphasizing the rapid evolution of AI technologies. The speaker reflects on past efforts, including experiments with MCP and retrieval‑augmented generation that exposed gaps in machine understanding and robustness. The presentation argues that judgment—not just raw data—is critical for AI systems to interpret federal statistics responsibly and highlights failures that demonstrate why structured metadata alone is insufficient. It introduces pragmatics as “the missing layer” needed to help machines navigate context, intent, and API behavior reliably. The talk stresses continued experimentation, adoption of tools such as WebMCP and llms.txt, and capturing expert knowledge before it is lost to workforce turnover. Best‑practice recommendations focus on making federal data more discoverable, more semantically structured, and better aligned to AI model workflows. Overall, the presentation frames AI‑ready data as an evolving challenge that requires technical, organizational, and epistemic shifts.

Title: Making Federal Data AI Ready:An Extension of Communicating Data Quality
Summary: This presentation outlines the evolution of federal data quality guidance and its extension into the realm of AI‑ready data, emphasizing the need for machine‑readable and machine‑understandable formats across statistical agencies. It connects earlier FCSM frameworks and the updated 2025 Data Quality Framework (DQF) to operational actions required for preparing federal datasets for modern generative AI systems, including baseline assessments, cross‑agency learning, and API and metadata modernization. A major focus is on the Model Context Protocol (MCP), which enables AI models to securely and contextually interact with federal data sources without bespoke integrations, vastly improving retrieval accuracy from 2.1% to as high as 95% in pilot implementations. The presentation highlights six persistent challenges—context awareness, scaling, discovery, governance, security, and evaluation—which require both technical and organizational solutions. It concludes by encouraging further adoption of MCP servers and collaborative practices to ensure federal data becomes more interpretable, discoverable, and actionable for AI use cases.

Title: From Statistical Data to Machine-Understandable Knowledge: Methodological Advances for AI Readiness in Federal Statistics
Summary: This presentation argues that AI readiness is now a methodological imperative for federal statistical agencies, emphasizing that AI systems require machine‑understandable statistical knowledge rather than human‑oriented metadata structures. It demonstrates how poorly structured metadata produce untrustworthy AI outputs and contrasts this with an AI‑ready example that incorporates survey identifiers, universes, geographies, variables, and margin‑of‑error information in fully structured form. The presenter outlines a three‑layer framework—validation, representation, and stewardship—that together enable semantic structuring optimized for AI consumption and cross‑survey integration, grounded in international metadata standards such as GSIM, DDI, and SDMX. A detailed knowledge‑graph model is introduced to show how AI systems traverse statistical meaning from concepts to data points, ensuring definitional fidelity and verifiable context for each datum retrieved. The talk also highlights the need for task‑adapted evaluation metrics to assess retrieval precision, reasoning consistency, and responsible AI behavior, noting that no single metric captures all dimensions of AI performance in statistical contexts. Ultimately, the presentation frames AI‑ready statistics as a coordinated governance effort embedding FAIR principles into federal statistical standards and integrating AI‑readiness into long‑term stewardship practices.

Title: Modernizing Access to NASS Quick Stats
Summary: This presentation describes efforts by the USDA National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS) to modernize access to its extensive Quickstats database by making data retrieval more conversational and accessible to non‑expert users. The team tested five different AI‑enabled approaches—Dual‑LLM RAG, Model Context Protocol (MCP), Google’s Data Commons, Azure Copilot Studio, and a fine‑tuned Databricks Genie—to determine which best balances accuracy, security, and cost in generating natural‑language interfaces to agricultural statistics. Early approaches such as RAG and MCP were powerful but vulnerable to prompt injection, tool poisoning, and high costs, while Data Commons required heavy schema work and offered non‑live data, and Copilot Studio posed customization and cost challenges. The final solution—a fine‑tuned Databricks Genie with a controlled API—yielded a highly accurate, context‑aware, and constrained system that minimizes risk and reduces marginal query costs. The presentation concludes with comparisons of security constraints, cost per query across methods, and open questions about validation, governance, and cross‑agency alignment for public‑facing AI systems.

Title: FCSM AI-Ready Data Working Group
Summary: This presentation describes the ongoing work of the FCSM AI‑Ready Data Working Group, a cross‑agency effort launched in 2025 to understand which metadata are most useful for improving AI-generated responses related to federal statistics. The group is exploring how AI systems use structured data and metadata when responding to user queries, especially in agent‑augmented model pipelines where metadata serve as context for disambiguation, ranking, and interpretation. Their research involves selecting several topic areas, assembling comprehensive survey‑, question‑, and table‑level metadata, formatting these into standardized prompts, and testing them across multiple AI services. They are evaluating the resulting model outputs for accuracy, relevance, clarity, inclusion of data quality indicators, and adherence to provided metadata. The presentation outlines challenges related to the evolving AI ecosystem—including reliance on pre‑training data, web search variability, and the future role of agent‑based architectures—and highlights the need for consistent metadata structures to support machine understanding. The presentation highlights the future release of a paper outlining the group's work.

Title: Building AI-Ready Best Practices: The Work of the Commerce Data Governance Board
Summary: The presentation outlines how the U.S. Census Bureau and the Department of Commerce are preparing public data assets to be “AI‑ready” amid rapid advancements in generative AI and large language models. It highlights shifting public expectations, historical changes in the data landscape, and the increasing need for structured, accessible, and well‑described data sources. The presenter demonstrates current challenges such as inaccurate AI‑generated responses that rely on secondary sources, underscoring the importance of improved data publishing tactics. Strategies emphasized include enhanced SEO and metadata practices, structured formats for easier ingestion, API‑based retrieval, and designing data products that meet AI systems where they currently are. The talk also showcases hybrid AI‑powered tools like the Census API Assistant GPT. Finally, the presentation stresses the importance of community engagement, open‑source collaborations, benchmarking, and ongoing ethical innovation.

Title: Unleashing the Power of Open Data - NOAA's AI Readiness Journey
Summary: This presentation describes NOAA’s efforts to make its extensive environmental data holdings AI‑ready through innovation, standardized data practices, and cloud modernization. It outlines NOAA’s mission, the breadth of its climate and environmental data products, and examples of AI applications such as detecting lightning, identifying whale calls, and monitoring marine debris. The NOAA Center for AI is leading the development of community standards for AI‑ready data and coordinating partnerships and training. NESDIS’ Common Cloud Framework (NCCF) is central to transforming and consolidating NOAA’s 30+ petabytes of data into cloud‑optimized formats that improve access, usability, and support for GenAI and traditional AI workflows. The presentation highlights challenges such as storage costs, diverse user needs, and the need to maximize return on investment, while emphasizing the opportunity presented by NOAA’s unique datasets. Pilot projects involve converting data to formats like Zarr, Cloud‑Optimized GeoTIFF, and STAC metadata to support scalable AI research. Overall, the talk frames AI readiness as both a technical modernization effort and a strategic opportunity for NOAA.

Title: AI-Ready DataThe Census Track to Machine Understandable Data
Summary: This presentation outlines a conceptual framework for making Census data truly “machine understandable,” emphasizing that modern AI systems require richer metadata and structured constraints rather than simple machine-readable formats. It reviews foundational definitions of AI and generative AI, noting recent advances that enable composite systems built from components trained on massive datasets. The presenter argues that what has fundamentally changed is the ability to integrate trained AI components into larger systems requiring iteration, experimentation, and genuine understanding. He introduces tiers of machine-understandable data, ranging from basic digital structure to table-level metadata, field-level metadata, and identity constraints needed for complex processing. The talk highlights the importance of data interdependencies, distributional expectations, and supporting non-scalar or compound data types. It also explores new possibilities such as democratized question answering, pedagogical interfaces, hybrid data products, knowledge-driven imputation, and interactive survey instruments. Overall, the presentation encourages reimagining data systems to support richer pipelines from data to insight to action.

Title: Look Before You Leap: Exploring BEA Data Capture by Generative AI Technologies
Summary: This presentation examines how generative AI tools interpret and present publicly available economic data from the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA). It describes BEA’s motivation for launching an AI Readiness project after observing that generative AI systems often return incorrect, incomplete, or inconsistently phrased responses about official statistics. The team tested 40 questions across major BEA directorates and found substantial accuracy problems, including misinterpretation of revised data and failures to return results. Findings showed that tools like ChatGPT and Google Gemini produced mixed outcomes, with many inaccurate or missing answers. The presentation emphasizes that these issues pose risks to public understanding of economic data. BEA plans to strengthen its understanding of how large language models retrieve information and is partnering with America’s DataHub Consortium to develop solutions enabling federal statistical products to be reliably represented by AI systems. The resulting solution will contribute to the National Secure Data Service, supporting broader federal use cases.

Title: Improving LLM Access to Federal Open Data: A Pilot Study of Model Context Protocol Servers for Federal Data Access
Author/Organization: Bella Mendoza, Mark Aronson, Haley Johnson, Sam Levy, Mohammed Arifur Rahman
Summary: This U.S. Digital Corps report evaluates how large language models (LLMs) access and interpret federal open data and finds that baseline retrieval accuracy is near‑zero—0% for USAspending and 2.1% for CDC PLACES—because current web interfaces and documentation are optimized for humans rather than machine understanding.  The authors test the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open standard for tool‑mediated AI interactions, and show that when MCP servers translate natural‑language queries into structured API calls, LLM performance improves dramatically—from 18% to 95% overall, including 100% accuracy on PLACES and 89.5% on USAspending.  They argue MCPs can “democratize” API access, mitigate reliance on unofficial sources, and enable authoritative, timely answers grounded in federal datasets.  Beyond the pilot, the paper recommends agency‑owned, open‑source MCP servers; a centralized discovery registry (potentially via Data.gov); and robust governance spanning security reviews, accuracy testing, and incident response.  Technical guidance covers server design (tool scoping, schema typing, paging), CI/CD and monitoring, and secure deployment practices to reduce risks like tool poisoning and shadowing.  The report situates this work within recent federal calls for “AI‑ready” data (e.g., FCSM guidance and Commerce best practices) and highlights MCPs’ potential to support internal agentic workflows such as document retrieval and compliance automation.  Overall, it positions MCP as essential infrastructure to make authoritative federal data reliably accessible to AI systems.

Title: Desirable Characteristics of Data Repositories for Federally Funded Research
Author/Organization: Subcommittee on Open Science of the National Science and Technology Council
Summary: This OSTP/NSTC guidance defines a consensus set of characteristics that data repositories should meet to support management and public access to data arising from U.S. federally funded research, emphasizing FAIR, equitable, secure, and trustworthy sharing.  The framework is organized across three themes—Organizational Infrastructure, Digital Object Management, and Technology—covering free and timely access, clear use guidance, risk management, retention, and long‑term sustainability; assignment of persistent identifiers (e.g., DOIs), community‑appropriate metadata, curation/QA, measured reuse, common (preferably non‑proprietary) formats, and documented provenance; plus authentication, long‑term technical sustainability, and cybersecurity aligned with established standards (e.g., NIST Cybersecurity Framework).  It adds a dedicated set of additional considerations for repositories storing human data, including fidelity to consent, tiered access and credentialing, limited‑use enforcement (e.g., anti‑reidentification), download control and auditing, transparent request review, breach response plans, and accountability mechanisms.  Agencies intend to use these characteristics to assist researchers in selecting repositories, to designate repositories for specific data types, and to evaluate data management plans, while avoiding formal certification mandates.  The document also aims to inform repository developers and future federal investments in open science infrastructure, anticipating updates as practices and technologies evolve.  Overall, it seeks consistent federal expectations that improve storage, discovery, reuse, and replication of research data and enhance stewardship of human‑subjects data.

Title: Data Cards for Standardized Metadata Across DOE-Aligned Data Initiatives
Summary: This DOE‑aligned technical report proposes a shared “Data Card”—a lightweight, extensible artifact that combines YAML front matter with Markdown narrative—to standardize dataset documentation for discovery, access, interoperability, reuse, governed use, and AI usability across heterogeneous programs.  It merges practices from Data Statements/Datasheets/Model Cards with public‑sector metadata standards, aligning key fields to DCAT 3.0/DCAT‑US, DataCite, and the ISO/IEC 11179 family while preserving domain‑specific extensions via a domain_metadata block.  The approach is paired with a LinkML schema and multi‑mode validation (Pydantic, JSON Schema, SHACL, SQL) to enforce required and conditional fields, controlled vocabularies, and structural consistency.  The card explicitly captures sensitivity and governance metadata (e.g., CUI, UCNI, export control, privacy/PII/PHI), distinguishes card vs. dataset visibility, and anticipates repository integration via American Science Cloud (AmSC) pipelines.  A relationship vocabulary and persistent identifiers link datasets to publications, software, and AI models, enabling provenance‑aware, FAIR, and AI‑ready workflows.  The report also describes authoring UX principles that surface only capability‑relevant fields, plus bi‑directional generation to and from narratives using LLM assistance.  Overall, it argues the Data Card should serve as a cross‑program metadata bridge that improves transparency, interoperability, and governed reuse without displacing repository‑native schemas or local review processes.

Title: Phase 2 Implementation of the Foundations for Evidence-Based Policymaking Act of 2018: Open Government Data Access and Management Guidance
Summary: This OMB guidance operationalizes the OPEN Government Data Act within the Evidence Act, rescinds M‑13‑13, and sets a systematic open‑data approach to bolster evidence‑building, AI innovation, research, and transparency while safeguarding privacy, confidentiality, and security.  It clarifies key categories (data, data assets, public data assets, open Government data assets), defines “make available,” and assigns implementation to Chief Data Officers (CDOs) and Data Governance Bodies.  Agencies must maintain comprehensive data inventories interoperable with the Federal Data Catalog (Data.gov) using DCAT‑US 3.0 metadata, post them at agency.gov/data.json, and update them within 90 days of asset creation and at least annually.  All agency data assets should be in open formats; public data assets must be machine‑readable, based on open standards, minimally restricted, and under an open license, with conversion and prioritization decisions guided by costs, benefits, and legal constraints.  Dissemination through Data.gov requires a structured risk‑balancing that considers national security, information security, privacy (including the mosaic effect and reidentification), intellectual property, contractual limits, and enables partial releases via disclosure‑limitation techniques.  Agencies must embed an open data plan in their IRM Strategic Plans covering collection in open formats, usage metrics, public engagement, points of contact, improvement processes, training/procurement, and prioritization criteria that explicitly include AI use cases.  The memo sets timelines—e.g., 180 days for updated plans and contact information, and September 30, 2026 for DCAT‑US 3.0 compliance, open formats, and open‑license requirements—while coordinating access pathways for non‑disseminated assets via FOIA and the Standard Application Process (SAP) under CIPSEA.

Title: Croissant: A Metadata Format for ML-Ready Datasets
Summary: The paper introduces Croissant, a schema.org‑based, JSON‑LD metadata format that makes machine learning datasets more discoverable, portable, and interoperable across tools, frameworks, and platforms.  It defines four layers—Dataset Metadata, Resources (FileObject and FileSet), Structure (RecordSet with Fields), and Semantics (splits, labels, common ML types)—to provide a unified, machine‑readable view without changing the underlying data layout. The ecosystem includes a Python library, TensorFlow Datasets (TFDS) CroissantBuilder, PyTorch DataPipes integration, a visual Croissant Editor, and support by major repositories (Hugging Face, Kaggle, OpenML) as well as Google Dataset Search.  A user study on ten popular datasets found high readability and understandability, good completeness, and moderate agreement (e.g., BLEU scores higher for Croissant core than Croissant‑RAI), with some annotator confusion between schema.org creator and publisher.  The paper also reports early adoption and “health” metrics for repository integrations and demonstrates semantic search over Croissant descriptions.  Limitations and future work include broader evaluation, enhanced tooling (e.g., the editor), and upcoming extensions such as Geo‑Croissant for complex geospatial formats.

Title: AI-Readiness of Data and Metadata for Official Statistics
Summary: This presentation covers how official statistics organizations can prepare data and metadata to be effectively used by generative AI systems, emphasizing that AI currently struggles to correctly extract, interpret, and attribute official statistics. It argues that official statisticians must improve both metadata (rich, structured, machine‑readable, API‑accessible) and data (checked, annotated, interpretable, machine‑readable) to make them AI‑ready. The presentation describes how AI can assist in anomaly detection, data annotation, metadata generation, metadata evaluation, and semantic search. It highlights the need for standards‑based metadata, enhanced discoverability through semantic search platforms, and better collaboration with data redistributors. Ultimately, it presents a division of labor where statisticians ensure data quality and metadata readiness while AI systems improve validation, documentation, and dissemination.

Title: Challenges and opportunities in effectively reaching users of official data and statistics in the AI era
Author/Organization: Dr. Eng Chuan Kh (Singapore Dept. of Statistics)
Summary: This presentation describes how the rise of AI systems as new, indirect users of official statistics creates challenges for national statistical offices (NSOs), including reduced visibility, misinterpretation, hallucination, inconsistent sourcing, and the widespread circulation of timely but inaccurate data. It uses case studies of youth unemployment estimates from multiple AI platforms to illustrate how different definitions, hidden sources, and varied prioritization lead to conflicting outputs. The presentation argues that NSOs must act as active agents of trusted data by designing outputs for both humans and machines, improving attribution, engaging more effectively with technology platforms and media, and investing in user education. It also emphasizes opportunities for productivity gains through better human–machine‑aligned dissemination and more agile communication strategies.

Title: From Open Data to Responsible Reuse: Hallmarks of Data Stewardship in the Age of AI
Author/Organization: Dr. Julia Stoyanovich (NYU Center for Responsible AI)
Summary: The presentation argues that open data must evolve into responsible reuse in the AI era, identifying five hallmarks of stewardship: data readiness, organizational readiness, technical readiness, stakeholder input, and validation and feedback.  It uses images and real‑world examples—including SingStat’s Chat with SANDRA, India’s eSankhyilki, and cautionary cases like NYC’s MyCity chatbot and tests of LLMs on government queries—to show how AI systems can misinform when provenance, definitions, revisions, and uncertainty are not preserved.  It illustrates loss of context with scenarios on Maldives GDP over time, SDG comparisons between Maldives and Burundi, and Serbia’s population, where territorial scope and methodological differences are flattened.  The author recommends developing AI‑ready metadata as machine‑readable, portable, dynamic “nutritional labels” that capture data, process, and result features, and that can be incrementally computable.  She calls for accountable data governance that mandates attribution, machine‑readable provenance, revision propagation, AI‑facing interfaces, and clear reuse conditions.  The presentation urges statistical offices to build organizational capacity and AI literacy, monitor AI‑mediated reuse, and collaborate across sectors.  It also emphasizes educating the public to interpret AI‑mediated statistics, understand uncertainty, and provide feedback.  Overall, the images and examples are integral, visually demonstrating both the risks of AI‑mediated dissemination and the features of stewardship that can make official data AI‑ready.

Title: AI-Ready Official Statistics: Opportunities, Challenges, and Recommendations
Summary: This paper examines how generative AI is transforming the dissemination and use of official statistics and introduces a framework for making statistical products “AI‑ready.”  Core components include comprehensive, machine‑readable metadata (with web‑optimized mappings), rigorous quality assurance and anomaly detection with value‑level annotations, interoperable API‑based delivery with open licensing, and improved discoverability strengthened by explicit signals of authoritativeness.  It identifies five interlinked challenges—proliferation of non‑official sources, AI‑mediated search and chatbots that reduce visibility and provenance, technical limitations of generative AI, weak partnerships with redistributors, and gaps in infrastructure, skills, and legal/ethical safeguards.  The document assigns roles and detailed recommendations to four stakeholder groups—national statistical organizations (NSOs), international/regional bodies, redistributors, and AI developers—to preserve integrity and trust in an AI‑enabled ecosystem.  For NSOs, priorities include adopting SDMX/DDI/ISO metadata standards and mapping to DCAT/schema.org/Croissant, automating anomaly detection and observation‑level annotations, modernizing dissemination with versioned APIs, semantic search, guarded chatbots, and machine‑readable release calendars, and investing in skills and secure platforms.  International bodies are urged to harmonize standards, publish templates and open tools for metadata and quality control, incubate semantic search and MCP‑enabled interfaces, build capacity in low‑ and middle‑income contexts, and broker partnerships and licensing guidance.  Redistributors should default to canonical sources, synchronize via APIs, retain attribution and metadata, use retrieval‑anchored generation with validation checks, and establish feedback loops, while AI developers should align with standards like SDMX, respect licenses and privacy, adopt responsible acquisition practices, and support low‑resource deployments; an annex highlights the Model Context Protocol as a promising pathway for safe, direct LLM integration with authoritative data.

Title: Fostering AI-Readiness and Responsible Redistribution of Official Statistics
Summary: This document argues that official statistics must become “AI‑ready” to remain accurate, discoverable, and trusted as AI‑enabled search engines and chatbots increasingly mediate access to data.  It diagnoses three core challenges—multiplicity of data sources, limited AI capability to interact with structured official data, and limited control over third‑party redistribution—illustrated by inconsistent AI answers to youth unemployment queries for Indonesia and Thailand.  The paper proposes Action 1 to modernize curation and dissemination via common metadata and exchange standards (e.g., SDMX), machine‑readable APIs, open licensing (CC BY 4.0), semantic search, a central catalog of accredited sources, and better LLM integration with structured databases (e.g., IMF StatGPT), alongside AI tools for anomaly detection and observation‑level annotations.  Action 2 calls for coordinated capacity building for data producers in low‑ and middle‑income countries to adopt these standards and practices.  Action 3 recommends guidance and collaboration with redistributors—covering proper attribution, provenance, transparency about transformations, feedback loops, and metadata mapping to schema.org and Croissant—so open data remains responsibly reused.  Grounded in the Fundamental Principles of Official Statistics, the document places responsibility on both producers and redistributors to uphold integrity, signal authoritativeness, and share usage insights to improve relevance and trust.

Title: Towards AI-Ready National Statistical Offices- A Framework for Strengthening NSO Capacity in Low- and Middle-Income Countries
A Practical Guide for NSOs The AI Readiness Self-Assessment
Guidelines and best practices for making government datasets ready for AI
Summary: This paper provides UK‑specific guidance for preparing government datasets to be “AI‑ready,” emphasizing that responsible AI adoption depends primarily on data quality, structure, governance, and legal clarity.  It presents a framework built around four pillars—technical optimization, data and metadata quality, organizational and infrastructure context, and legal, security, and ethical compliance—and details essential capabilities within each.  The document highlights common barriers such as inconsistent metadata, legacy systems, fragmented standards, unclear legal bases, and organizational accountability gaps.  Through interviews with major public bodies like DWP, NHS, i.AI, and The National Archives, it identifies practical challenges and showcases examples of good practice, including lakehouse architectures, federated learning, synthetic data use, and preservation‑grade metadata.  The paper underscores the need to treat datasets as strategic products and to maintain continuous oversight through robust governance, documentation, and monitoring.  It concludes that AI readiness cannot be assessed with a universal checklist but must be evaluated per dataset, use case, and organizational context, supported by a self‑assessment model.

Title: A framework for AI-ready data
Summary: This paper presents the Open Data Institute’s practical framework for making datasets AI‑ready, emphasizing that high‑quality, well‑documented, standards‑aligned data is essential for reliable and responsible AI systems.  The ODI identifies four components of AI‑readiness—technical optimization, data quality and standards, legal compliance, and responsible collection—and argues that existing frameworks such as FAIR, FAIR‑R, and sector‑specific AI‑readiness models lack sufficient operational detail for data publishers.  The report provides detailed criteria for dataset properties, metadata requirements, and surrounding infrastructure, including use of international standards, consistent labeling, machine‑readable metadata, comprehensive lifecycle documentation, and accessible APIs.  It incorporates insights from expert interviews to highlight practical issues such as metadata gaps, inconsistent formats, unclear supply‑chain provenance, and the need for stronger governance, which was added in the updated 2025 version of the framework.  The paper demonstrates the framework through structured assessments of two example datasets, illustrating how the criteria help diagnose strengths and deficiencies in AI‑readiness.  Ultimately, the report positions AI‑ready data practices as holistic, iterative, and collaborative, requiring ongoing dialogue between data publishers and AI practitioners.  It concludes that adopting these practices not only supports AI development but also improves overall data stewardship and utility across the broader data ecosystem.

Title: AI-ready data action plan
Summary: This UK guidance defines what AI‑ready data means for government and sets a practical framework to prepare public‑sector datasets for responsible AI use, emphasizing quality, documentation, governance, and usability.  It organizes best practices into four pillars; technical optimisation, data & metadata quality, organization & infrastructure context, and legal, security & ethical compliance and ties them to actionable steps and success criteria that build on FAIR principles.  An embedded AI‑Ready Data Action Plan maps departmental insights and key challenges across pillars, covering modern machine‑readable formats, APIs, scalable infrastructure, provenance‑rich metadata, stewardship roles, and proportionate security controls.  The guidance highlights common barriers (siloed data, uneven documentation, unclear ownership) and calls for structured metadata, transparent data lineage, and human‑in‑the‑loop oversight to strengthen trust and accountability.  It positions the framework within a broader AI agenda (including playbooks and ethics guidance) to ensure datasets are accurate, complete, consistent, secure, and enriched with context for both humans and machines.  Overall, it aims to unlock AI value in public services by standardizing how government prepares, governs, and shares datasets for AI, while updating the guidance as practices and technologies evolve.

Title: From open data to AI-ready data: Building the foundations for responsible AI in development
Summary: This World Bank blog argues that the open data era must evolve into AI‑ready data, defined as development data that are consistently discoverable, comprehensible, accessible, and usable by both humans and AI systems—so AI can reliably return authoritative, up‑to‑date insights rather than hallucinations or outdated results.  AI‑ready data builds on existing standards and principles (e.g., open data frameworks and FAIR) rather than replacing them, emphasizing structured documentation, validation, and responsible sharing.  The post outlines three pillars for AI‑readiness: (1) AI‑ready data systems (discovery platforms, APIs, technical standards), (2) high‑quality data & metadata (comprehensive, structured, current), and (3) robust governance & strategic partnerships to ensure integrity, transparency, and responsible use.  It highlights practical steps such as hybrid semantic/lexical search, machine‑readable standards (e.g., SDMX) with well‑documented APIs, open licensing, and emerging interoperability protocols like the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to help AI identify and interpret trusted sources.  The authors situate this within the Bank’s AI for Data – Data for AI program, which applies AI to improve metadata, discovery, anomaly detection, and monitoring of data use while structuring datasets so AI can consume them responsibly.  Overall, the message is that making development data AI‑ready will shorten the distance between data and decision‑making, democratize access to credible evidence, and strengthen public trust in AI‑enabled development insights.

Title: Introducing the Open Knowledge Format
Author/Organization: Sam McVeety and Amir Hormati (Google Data Cloud)
Summary: This blog entry from staff at Google, in addition to its related specification (https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/knowledge-catalog/blob/main/okf/SPEC.md), outline a standard for representing metadata, context, and curated knowledge that can be used with modern AI systems. This framework represents knowledge as markdown files with YAML headers and some agreed-upon conventions that would allow models to easily navigate and consume the information contained within them. The authors liken this to maintaining an internal wiki. The authors also highlight the benefits of the proposed system. Namely, OKF does not require third-party software to produce, it does not require additional tooling to render or make use of, it is simple text that can be version controlled, and it is human AND machine readable. The OKF exists as a folder full of markdown files with a folder structure that matches the hierarchy of concepts you are trying to express (referred to as a bundle). Each markdown file represents a concept. Concepts can be linked through markdown style links to other files in the folder structure. The authors expect the specification to evolve as more adopt it and submit amendments.

Title: AI - Ready Data Demistified
Summary: A conference session examining whether "AI-ready data" names a real practice distinct from data quality. Orr adopts a definition for AI-readiness via Gemini: "AI-ready data is high quality, clean, structured, and securely governed information that can be immediately used by AI applications to train models, generate insights, or drive automation without requiring extensive preprocessing," characterized by "accuracy, proper labeling, and semantic context" — clarifying that this "means the preprocessing happened before the data became AI-ready, not that we don't preprocess." There are five pillars of AI-ready data: high quality and clean; structured and labeled; contextualized with metadata sufficient "to understand the source and the destination of this data"; governed and secured; and accessible and connected to the AI initiatives being run. Two conditions distinguish this from classical data quality — multimodality, because "we now have our files, text files, documents, images, meeting recordings," and use-case dependence, since "everything in AI is use case dependent" and "for each such case, our requirements from the data and our definition to what is good or bad or complete would change." Making data AI ready is a six-part process: define and validate requirements per use case, control performance and cost, version the data, run continuous regression testing (validation as "the CI for the data," production monitoring as "the CD for the data"), govern and secure, and instrument observability — all under the repeated formula "implement, validate, and then monitor."

Title: From the AI Trenches: Lessons Learned Building Infrastructure for AI-Ready Data
Author/Organization: Paul Dix, Shirshanka Das, and Guy Korland
Summary: A practitioner panel on why AI initiatives stall between experimentation and production. The panelists consider data to be AI ready when: it is discoverable, the quality is monitored and updated regularly, access to it is controlled, it has clear ownership, technical documentation provides information about the data’s provenance and metadata provides enough context to guide AI on how to use and interpret it.  On becoming AI ready, the panel recommends a bottom-up strategy instead of top-down. Start bottom-up with a small proven project rather than a top-down mandate, since organizations given "an order from the top down" mostly failed. Build even the first pilot with "a little bit of platform thinking, and a little bit of shared infrastructure mindset"; start from outcomes and "back into what data do we need"; instrument selectively rather than collecting everything; and audit continuously, because data curation resembles code refactoring — "it's a continuous process that you do again and again."

Title: Realizing the Value of AI: Cisco AI Readiness Index 2025
Summary: Very few organizations are realizing value from their AI investments. The ones that do invest across six pillars simultaneously: strategy, infrastructure, data, governance, talent, and culture. Furthermore, they maintain their AI-readiness by doing so continuously. Cisco defines the most successful organizations as Pacesetters because they plan and act with clarity, invest in infrastructure early, treat data as a discipline (keeping it “clean, centralized, and ready to integrate”), lead transformation rather than technology with change management built in, and balance innovation with guardrails. AI Infrastructure debt is an emerging threat to organizations who cut corners while making AI investments across the six pillars. This is defined as "the accumulation of gaps, trade-offs, short-cuts and lags in compute, networking, data management, security, and talent that compound as companies rush to deploy AI." The authors come to these conclusions using responses from Cisco’s 2025 survey measuring organizational AI readiness and its relationship to realized value. The sample included 8,039 business leaders at organizations with 500 or more employees across 30 markets and 26 industries.

Title: Department of Commerce: Generative AI & Open Government Data Assets
Summary: Deloitte names AI-ready data as the top tier of a four-level taxonomy it builds itself: raw products, then conformed, then BI-ready, then AI-ready, where "the AI models require context along with the data" and datasets "undergo cleaning and organizing the data, tagged and categorized appropriately." What separates AI-ready from BI-ready is context, not cleanliness. Its path has three parts. One secure cloud environment spanning bureaus, plus managed metadata, together "will give Commerce the foundation required to make your data AI Ready." Each subject-matter team then publishes and maintains its own datasets the way a software team ships a product, with a small central team setting standards. AI Readiness at the organizational level is a maturity model. It climbs a crawl-walk-run-fly ladder as it matures. Crawl is ad hoc and manual, the organization can walk when processes are more defined at the foundational level and are automated. In the run stage, the organization standardizes use cases and they become pervasive at the enterprise level. When it can fly, the organization leverages the work it has already done to embrace next-generation capabilities.

Title: Leidos
Author/Organization: Response to the Department of Commerce AI and Open Government Data Assets Request for Information
Summary: Leidos adopts Gartner’s definition of AI readiness: "...data that has met AI readiness requirements for an AI use case, tailored to a specific AI technique's need." Readiness is also a function of its use case, “...the data criteria for a generative AI use case significantly differs from those for a predictive model.” Those building AI solutions must ensure data are AI-ready for their application. Before anyone can use Commerce data in an AI system they must first acquire, clean, reshape, bias-check, label and patch it. This can take a few weeks to several months. work Leidos says "can take a few weeks to several months" and calls the "data processing chasm." Leidos recommends six ways for Commerce to make its data ready for AI. Standardize individual fields, not just file formats. Allow users to request the units, dates, and times zones they need at the download instead of fixing them afterwards. Use AI to help prep data. Publish what the data look like, where it came from, how often it changes, and how its categories are defined. Ship formats a program can read without a person in the loop. Give users a way to report problems and provide other feedback.

Title: Microsoft
Author/Organization: Response to the Department of Commerce AI and Open Government Data Assets Request for Information
Summary: Microsoft provides a series of recommendations for the government to make its data ready for AI researchers to use. Researchers cannot get the data (accessibility), cannot find it (discoverability), and cannot use it without heavy rework (usability). On accessibility it asks Commerce to publish unstructured material by default, meaning "all text, audio, images, and videos that are categorized as public records," and to ship early rather than perfect first: "data should not be held back from accessibility to first improve its other qualities, such as metadata or formatting." It sets a spending order, with the highest return on assets "already digital but not available online," then hard-to-find online assets, then digitizing paper. On discoverability it asks Commerce to stop blocking web crawlers, publish data dictionaries defining "data fields, units, and relationships," publish API documentation, invest in search and filtering for the largest holdings such as SEC Edgar and Data.gov, keep building curated landing pages, and use AI for discovery so a user can ask "what data is relevant for training an AI model on sign language recognition" and get back relevant databases. On usability it asks Commerce to keep the original file, since "the most valuable and useable long-term format will not necessarily be easy to predict" and a publishing institution "need not" convert, while producing JSON or XML versions of the few datasets in heavy demand; to ship script-friendly formats like CSV and plain text; to build sites for machines with structured markup and valid certificates; to make bulk and filtered downloads work, video being hardest; to link documents to each other rather than only tagging them individually; and to disclose provenance with "tags that show whether bias analysis was conducted or not." It then splits metadata requirements between raw data (descriptive, structural, administrative, real-time) and derived data (descriptive, provenance, quality, usage), recommends the Linux Foundation's Community Data License Agreement or CC BY, and names DCAT, schema.org, OpenAPI, FGDC and OGC. A closing framework has no counterpart in the docket: valuable training text is authoritative, unique, knowledge and logic dense, recent or still relevant, and long-context.

Title: OpenAI
Author/Organization: Response to the Department of Commerce AI and Open Government Data Assets Request for Information
Summary: OpenAI prescribes six properties that public data files should have: a program should be able to read only the columns it needs. It should be readable in any language (python, C++, etc.). It should be small on disk. It should carry its own field definitions. Adding a field should not break the programs already reading it. And a shared standard should govern all of this, a job OpenAI assigns to NIST. OpenAI also recommends continuing to have data federated across the government since "there may not be an effective way to create a single, standardized repository." Raw and derived data serve different purposes, and for pre-training "qualitative data that represents language or human perception of the world is more valuable." Commerce should also ensure access to a wide diversity of sources since broad training produces a model "like a person who has been exposed to a wide range of cultural perspectives."

Title: Protesero
Author/Organization: Response to the Department of Commerce AI and Open Government Data Assets Request for Information
Summary: Protesero offers recommendations grounded in the belief that AI readiness begins with quality data and that technology alone cannot substitute for sound data management practices. Drawing on their experience with data-centric and human-centric approaches, Protesoro argues that achieving truly AI-ready open data at scale requires a foundation built on semantic metadata, clear data ownership, and iterative governance — all supported by modern tools such as data catalogs, knowledge graphs, and open data formats like JSON, Parquet, and Iceberg. The response emphasizes that pre-processing, labeling, and ontological enrichment must precede AI deployment, and that humans — particularly domain experts — must remain active partners throughout the data lifecycle. Protesoro further contends that AI-ready data must be accessible to all citizens, not just technical professionals, and that diversity in training data is essential to mitigating bias. On the topics of security, ethics, and governance, the response points to NIST's AI Risk Management Framework and related publications as the appropriate guidance frameworks, while cautioning that unconscious human bias risks being embedded into AI systems without proper oversight. Taken together, Protesoro's recommendations reflect a view that the path to responsible, high-quality open data for AI use is not primarily a technical challenge, but an organizational and human one.

Title: SAS Response to AI and Ope nGovernment Data Assets RFI
Summary:
To ensure that data accessible, usable, trustworthy, and safe for AI applications, SAS Institute argues that resolving this challenge requires treating AI readiness as the convergence of three interdependent conditions: high-quality, well-governed data; comprehensive and accurate metadata; and a strong ethical foundation. Central to this framing is the recognition that data labeled "AI-ready" carries an implicit public trust obligation — because AI systems and their users will assume such data has been vetted for bias and is fit for purpose, the consequences of releasing poorly prepared data are not merely technical but social. Data quality, in SAS's definition, is the set of formalized processes ensuring data conforms to business definitions and associated business rules across four dimensions — Business Definition, Data Element, Data Record, and Data Movement — and must be actively managed through centralized governance, service level agreements, and continuous monitoring performed as close to the data source as possible.

To achieve this standard, SAS recommends that Commerce develop a comprehensive, integrated data strategy spanning five areas: open, well-documented dissemination standards that prevent AI hallucinations; user-centered data portals designed for a broad range of users; structured government-industry-academic collaboration through mechanisms like Reverse Industry Days; data integrity practices grounded in the SAS Data Management Framework — which explicitly cautions against knowledge graphs in favor of more scalable encoding and dimension reduction techniques — and an ethical framework that embeds privacy protection, bias mitigation, and equitable access at every stage of the data lifecycle. Taken together, SAS argues that the technical and ethical dimensions of AI readiness are inseparable: without governance, metadata, and ethics working in concert, even well-formatted data will produce AI outcomes that are unreliable, inequitable, and unworthy of public trust.

Title: AI - Ready Data Essentials: How to Govern, Qualify, and Align Data to Deliver Value with AI
Summary: Gartner argues that in order for data to be ready for AI, it must be representative of the use case, “of every partner,errors, outliers and unexpected emergence that is needed to train or run the AI model for the specific use.” The path to AI-readiness is not a one-time operation, but a process and practice based on the extent to which the organization has metadata to align, qualify, and govern the data. They also walk readers through a five-stage path: 1) Assessing data management readiness, 2) Getting buy-in from the board, 3) Evolving the data management practices, 4) Extending the data management ecosystem, and 5) Scaling the operation and Setting up a governance system.

Title: CDO Insights 2026: Data Governance and the Trust Paradox of Data and AI Literacy Take Center Stage
Summary: A survey of data leaders at large corporations across the world report accelerating their efforts to bring Generative AI into their business practices while exhibiting major risks to making it successful. 69% of Chief Data Officers, Chief Data and AI Officers, and Chief Analytics Officers survey reported speeding up introducing GenAI and another 25% expecting to do so in the next 12 months. Data leaders' responses to the survey showed that data is paramount to making AI initiatives successful, as 61% cite better data making it easier to transition GenAI pilots to production and 50% pointing to data quality issues as a to challenge. Leaders are also concerned that their employees put too much faith into their organization’s data quality and the quality of GenAI products because they lack sufficient data and AI literacy. Thus, roughly ¾ of data leaders believe that their workforce needs to upskill in data and AI in order to use AI and AI products in day-to-day operations. About half of data leaders are investing in training their current staff or hiring more data and AI fluent staff to guard against such pitfalls. Most data leaders also report working to improve data and AI workflows, investing to improve data quality, and investing in data and metadata collection and management to improve the success rates of their GenAI pilots.

Title: Understanding AI Readiness Before Implementation with Tim Gasper and Juan Sequeda
Summary: The host, Molly Presley, speaks with Tim Gasper, Senior Director of Outbound Product Management at ServiceNow, and Juan Sequeda, Principal Researcher for Data and Analytics at ServiceNow, about what it means for enterprises to be truly ready for AI. Their central claim is that successful enterprise AI depends not on access to powerful models, but on a foundation of trusted, well-governed, semantically rich data — because AI agents, unlike human workers, lack the contextual knowledge needed to interpret enterprise data accurately. To build that foundation, they argue, organizations must tie AI initiatives directly to measurable business objectives, balance bottom-up infrastructure investment with top-down business priorities, and adopt a product management mindset that treats data and AI outputs as managed assets with clear ownership, quality standards, and defined consumers. They further contend that the enterprises most likely to succeed over the next 12 to 24 months will be those that move beyond simply deploying general-purpose AI tools and instead embed AI-powered workflows directly into core business processes — an achievement made possible only when metadata, governance, and context management are treated not as compliance exercises, but as strategic enablers of scalable, compounding value.

Title: The Missing Layer: Why Semantics and Knowledge Graphs Are Essential for AI-Ready Data Systems
Summary: Despite the recent surge of interest in knowledge graphs and large language models, the hard problem of AI readiness remains largely unsolved — not because organizations lack AI tools, but because their data lacks meaning. This presentation argues that the missing ingredient is governed metadata: the deliberate codification of business terminology, its mapping to physical data structures, and its organization into ontologies that AI systems can actually use. Benchmark results bear this out, showing up to 4x gains in query accuracy when LLMs are given a semantically rich knowledge graph instead of a raw SQL schema. Drawing on decades of work in semantic web standards and knowledge representation, much of it predating the current AI boom, the presentation walks through a practical framework for building what the author calls an "enterprise brain": a knowledge graph that connects data, people, business processes, and domain concepts into a single, reusable source of organizational truth. The lesson from early adopters like S&P Global is straightforward: AI readiness is not about the tools you deploy, it is about whether your data means something before it gets there.

Title: AI Data Readiness Inspector (AIDRIN) for Quantitative Assessment of Data Readiness for AI
Author/Organization: Kaveen Hiniduma, Suren Byna, Jean Luca Bez, and Ravi Madduri
Publication: 6th International Conference on Scientific and Statistical Database Management (SSDBM 2024), July 10–12, 2024, Rennes, France
Summary: This article introduces AIDRIN (AI Data Readiness INspector), a unified framework designed to quantitatively and qualitatively assess the "readiness" of datasets for artificial intelligence applications. To address the limitations of disjointed data quality tools, AIDRIN integrates traditional data quality metrics (completeness, outliers, duplicates) with specialized AI-specific evaluations, such as feature importance, correlations, class imbalance, fairness, privacy, and FAIR principle compliance. Built using Python, the framework simplifies the evaluation pipeline by offering user-friendly visualizations and exportable JSON reports to help researchers and data scientists make informed preprocessing decisions.
Tags (comma separated): data readiness metrics, data quality assessment, data readiness for AI, FAIR principles

Title: A RAG data pipeline transforming heterogeneous data into AI-ready format for autonomous building performance discovery
Author/Organization: Han Li, Ana Comesana, Christopher Weyandt, and Tianzhen Hong
Publication: Advances in Applied Energy  (Volume 21, 2026), available online December 31, 2025
Summary: This study addresses the persistent data challenges in the building sector, where integrating and understanding heterogeneous and unstructured building documentation is highly labor-intensive. The authors present a domain-adapted Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) data pipeline that uses Large Language Models (LLMs) and tailored document preprocessing (optimized for plain text, images, and tables) to convert raw building artifacts into semantically rich, AI-ready representations. The pipeline demonstrates a 30% improvement in metadata coverage and structural preservation over generic baselines and significantly reduces the manual effort required to generate semantic building models (like Brick Schema).
Tags (comma separated): retrieval augmented generation (RAG), Building performance, Data discovery

Title: Data Readiness for Scientific AI at Scale
Author/Organization: Wesley Brewer, Patrick Widener, Valentine Anantharaj, Feiyi Wang, Tom Beck, Arjun Shankar, and Sarp Oral
Publication: 54th International Conference on Parallel Processing Companion (ICPP Companion ’25), September 08–11, 2025, San Diego, CA
Summary: This paper examines how Data Readiness for AI (DRAI) principles apply to leadership-scale scientific datasets used to train foundation models. The authors analyze preprocessing patterns across four high-performance computing (HPC) research domains—climate, nuclear fusion, bio/health, and materials science. To standardize the conversion of raw scientific inputs into ready-to-train deep learning formats, they introduce a two-dimensional conceptual maturity framework that bridges operational Data Readiness Levels (from raw to AI-ready) with core scientific Data Processing Stages (ingest, preprocess, transform, structure, shard).
Tags (comma separated): climate science, fusion research, bioinformatics, materials science

Title: Transforming Big Data into AI-ready data for nutrition and obesity research
Author/Organization: Diana M. Thomas, Rob Knight, Jack A. Gilbert, Marilyn C. Cornelis, Marie G. Gantz, Kate Burdekin, Kevin Cummiskey, Susan C. J. Sumner, Wimal Pathmasiri, Edward Sazonov, Kelley Pettee Gabriel, Erin E. Dooley, Mark A. Green, Andrew Pfluger, and Samantha Kleinberg
Publication: Obesity (Silver Spring) (Volume 32, Issue 5), Published in May 2024
Summary: This review explores how Big Data (microbiome, metabolomics, and accelerometry) is increasingly leveraged in precision nutrition and obesity research to formulate personalized recommendations. However, raw biological and sensor streams are not directly usable and require labor-intensive preprocessing. The paper details the specialized software, validation pipelines, and critical points where human judgment or parameters (such as managing missing values, batch effects, and epoch settings) impact final AI-ready products. The authors argue that transparency in these data foundation steps is essential to avoid faulty clinical interpretations downstream.
Tags (comma separated): preprocessing pipelines, metabolomics, accelerometry, quality control

Title: Advancing FAIR data towards comparable, organized, predictive AI-ready data for community validation
Author/Organization: Elisha M. Wood-Charlson, Wolmar N. Åkerström, Lindsey Anderson, Mikayla A. Borton, Stephen K. Burley, Neil Byers, Ishwar Chandramouliswaran, Sylvain V. Costes, Paramvir S. Dehal, Mitchel Doktycz, Emiley Eloe-Fadrosh, Christopher Henry, Kjiersten Fagnan, Oliver Fiehn, Mahantesh Halappanavar, Bonnie Hurwitz, Marcin P. Joachimiak, Sean Jungbluth, Julia Koblitz, Gazi Mahmud, Lee Ann McCue, Thomas O. Metz, Nigel Mouncey, Christopher J. Mungall, Tiffanie M. Nelson, Valerie Skye, Amanda M. Saravia-Butler, V. Ratna Saripalli, Susannah G. Tringe, Tim Van Den Bossche, and Adam P. Arkin
Summary: While the scientific community has widely adopted the FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) data principles for individual static datasets, integrating these disparate resources for large-scale meta-analysis and machine learning remains highly manual, fragmented, and time-consuming. To address this, the authors propose expanding the existing framework to FAIR + COPE (Comparable, Organized, Predictive, Engaged).  This framework turns data curation into an active, iterative scientific process where datasets are standardized into comparable units, structured systematically to capture inferred relationships, linked transparently to their origin/provenance, and continuously validated and updated by an engaged, active community. The article highlights several platform resources (such as KBase, BV-BRC, and GBIF) and real-world scientific use cases (such as bacterial phenotype prediction and the GROWdb river microbiome catalog) to demonstrate how adopting the automated, iterative FAIR + COPE process accelerates the generation of truly AI-ready data for predictive modeling.
Tags (comma separated): FAIR + COPE, Comparable, Organized, Predictive, Engaged

Title: AI-ready Data in Solar Physics and Space Science: Concerns, Mitigation and Recommendations
Author/Organization: Bala Poduval, R. L. McPherron, R. Walker, M. D. Himes, K. M. Pitman, A. R. Azari, C. Shneider, A. K. Tiwari, S. Kapali, G. Bruno, M. Georgoulis, O. Verkhoglyadova, J. Borovsky, G. Lapenta, J. Liu, T. Alberti, P. Wintoft, S. Wing, and R. Shuping
Publication: This white paper was inspired by discussions at the virtual international conference, “Applications of Statistical Methods and Machine Learning in the Space Sciences” (held 17-21 May 2021), and references its published proceedings in a Frontiers topical collection in 2022
Summary: This paper addresses the critical need and urgency to establish standards for "AI-readiness" in space science and heliophysics data. While ground-based and space-borne instruments have accumulated massive volumes of data, preparing this data for artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and deep learning (DL) applications remains a primary challenge.

Title: Leveraging Microsoft Fabric Lakehouse as an AI-Ready Data Platform for Enterprise Analytics
Publication: Journal of Information Systems Engineering and Management
Summary: Enterprises generate massive, constantly changing streams of structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data, but data science teams routinely spend the majority of their time on tedious data discovery, cleaning, and preparation before AI models can be trained or deployed. This paper examines Microsoft Fabric Lakehouse as a unified, cloud-native case study for building an "AI-ready" data platform. By integrating key structural components—such as Data Factory for ingestion, Synapse Data Engineering, Synapse Data Science for automated machine learning, and Power BI for real-time visualization—Fabric manages the entire MLOps lifecycle within a decoupled, highly efficient compute-and-storage architecture. Crucially, the paper explores how organizations must balance technical performance and cloud cost governance with robust enterprise ecosystems that enforce data lineage, metadata cataloging, compliance, and strict privacy controls. Real-world manufacturing and telecommunications case studies are provided to demonstrate how this architecture drastically reduces processing bottleneck times and scales operational analytics.
Tags (comma separated): data engineering, foundation model, governance, privacy, regulation, regulatory compliance

Title: Moving Toward the FAIR-R principles: Advancing AI-Ready Data
Author/Organization: Stefaan Verhulst, Andrew Zahuranec, and Hannah Chafetz
Summary: While the traditional FAIR principles have long guided scientific open data management, they do not natively address the unique, demanding requirements of modern artificial intelligence. The authors introduce the FAIR-R framework, which expands the classic principles to explicitly include Readiness for AI. Under this framework, datasets must be systematically formatted, structured, and labeled to support downstream machine learning and generative AI workflows—such as pretraining foundational models, adapting models for domain-specific tasks, and generating synthetic data. The paper maps out the "fourth wave of open data," which transitions from simply making datasets open to optimizing them for impactful, purpose-driven reuse. To successfully transition to this wave and avoid a potential "Data Winter," the authors argue that the global community must adopt advanced data-handling standards—including robust provenance tracking, data contracts, and sector-specific metadata—while resolving ongoing governance challenges surrounding equitable access, data commons, and ethical/legal compliance.
Tags (comma separated): AI ecosystem, data labeling, provenance tracking, data standards, governance models, open data

Title: A roadmap to artificial intelligence (AI): Methods for designing and building AI ready data to promote fairness
Author/Organization: Farah Kidwai-Khan, Rixin Wang, Melissa Skanderson, Cynthia A. Brandt, Samah Fodeh, and Julie A. Womack
Publication: Journal of Biomedical Informatics, available online May 11, 2024
Summary: AI and machine learning applications in healthcare are highly vulnerable to algorithmic bias, which can lead to discriminatory patient care and unequal health recommendations. Because biased outputs stem directly from flawed inputs, the authors present a clinical data-preparation roadmap to actively mitigate bias and promote equity before applying AI algorithms. Using Veterans Affairs (VA) electronic health records (EHR), they demonstrate rigorous preprocessing techniques across two clinical studies: machine learning to predict patient falls and natural language processing (NLP) to extract bone-density T-scores from dual x-ray absorptiometry (DXA) scans. The authors highlight how "raw" unstructured health records often contain missing demographic details, skewed representations of minority populations, and fragmented data across regional sites. By linking multi-site records, applying clinical-expert-validated definitions, imputing missing demographic variables (such as race and ethnicity), and carefully managing text snippet extraction, they generated highly accurate, clean, and representative datasets. The paper outlines actionable recommendations to institutionalize these practices, such as diversifying research team demographics, validating cleaning procedures across cohorts, and sharing code for transparency.

Title: The Impact of Data and AI on Scientific Production
Author/Organization: Barend Mons (Professor of Biosemantics at Leiden University Medical Center), Arie Baak (Lead Data Scientist, Euretos), and Koen Jonkers (Joint Research Centre, European Commission).
Summary: Co-authored by Barend Mons (one of the original authors of the FAIR principles), this policy paper analyzes why standard FAIR-compliant open data is no longer enough in the age of generative models. It advocates for the new "FAIR² (FAIR Squared)" framework, designed to make scientific research completely machine-actionable, context-rich, and Fully AI-Ready (AIR) while ensuring data sovereignty.

Title: scCompass: An Integrated Multi-Species scRNA-seq Database for AI-Ready
Author/Organization: Pengfei Wang, Wenhao Liu, Jiajia Wang, Yana Liu, Pengjiang Li, Ping Xu, Wentao Cui, Ran Zhang, Qingqing Long, Zhilong Hu, Chen Fang, Jingxi Dong, Chunyang Zhang, Yan Chen, Chengrui Wang, Guole Liu, Hanyu Xie, Yiyang Zhang, Meng Xiao, Shubai Chen, Haiping Jiang, The X-Compass Consortium, Yiqiang Chen, Ge Yang, Shihua Zhang, Zhen Meng, Xuezhi Wang, Guihai Feng, Xin Li, and Yuanchun Zhou
Summary: The article introduces scCompass, a highly efficient and scalable, multi-species single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) database designed specifically to support artificial intelligence (AI) model training. While single-cell sequencing technologies have generated massive amounts of data, utilizing these resources for machine learning remains challenging due to inconsistent processing quality and standardizations.  To address these hurdles, the authors processed over 2 petabytes of raw public transcriptomic data using a unified pipeline.

Title: AI-Ready Data Infrastructure: A Review of Zero-ETL, Declarative Pipelines, and Data Contracts in Modern Data Engineering
Publication: Cognizance Journal of Multidisciplinary Studies, Vol. 5, Issue. 8, August 2025
Summary: This article reviews how the rapid growth of artificial intelligence and machine learning has exposed the latency, fragility, and scalability limitations of traditional batch-oriented Extract-Transform-Load (ETL) systems. To meet the real-time demands of AI workloads, the author examines a core triad of emerging paradigms: Zero-ETL (which bypasses pre-processing using schema-on-read and event-driven ingestion), Declarative Pipelines (which replace imperative scripts with outcome-oriented orchestration), and Data Contracts (which establish formal producer-consumer agreements for data quality and governance). The paper surveys tools across these domains—such as Snowflake, dbt, and Dagster—and outlines open research challenges, including schema drift management, automated contract enforcement, and the lack of academic validation frameworks and standardized benchmarks.
Tags (comma separated): ETL (Extract Transfer Load), Zero-ETL Architecture, Declarative Data Pipelines, Schema Drift, Data Governance

Title: Building an AI-Ready Data Strategy Using Lakehouse Technology
Publication: Journal of Computer Science and Technology Studies, Vol. 7, Issue 3, May 2025 (Published May 8, 2025)
Summary: This article explores how organizations can leverage data lakehouse technology to unify the flexibility and low storage cost of data lakes with the reliability and ACID transaction support of data warehouses. The author argues that lakehouses serve as an ideal foundation for enterprise AI strategies by streamlining data ingestion, preparation, metadata management, governance, and scalable infrastructure. The paper highlights applications such as predictive analytics, recommendation engines, natural language processing, and automated decision-making, while addressing implementation challenges related to data quality, governance at scale, and cost management.
Tags (comma separated): unified data management, data governance, scalable infrastructure

Title: The metadata ecosystem and AI: Enabling FAIR and AI-ready data
Author/Organization: Jane Greenberg, Joel Pepper, Xintong Zhao, Richard Marciano, David Breen, and Yuan An
Publication: AI Magazine, Vol. 47, e70060, 2026 (Received October 16, 2025; Accepted April 21, 2026)
Summary: This article examines the bidirectional relationship between metadata and artificial intelligence, treating metadata both as foundational infrastructure that enables AI and as an output refined by AI-driven processes. The authors frame the metadata ecosystem around four key standard categories: data structure, data value, data encoding, and data syntax. Through four case studies—covering AI-ready biodiversity specimen images, extraction recipes for metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), a MOF knowledge graph, and a conversational archival research assistant ("ChatLoS")—the article demonstrates how high-quality, FAIR-aligned metadata supports reproducibility, enforces structured constraints, reduces LLM hallucinations, and ensures AI readiness.

Title: The Role of Metadata in Making Data AI-Ready: Enhancing Data Discoverability and Usability
Publication: Journal of Computer Science and Technology Studies, Vol. 7, Issue 5, June 2025 (Published June 10, 2025)
Summary: This paper investigates the critical role of descriptive, structural, and administrative metadata in preparing enterprise data for artificial intelligence applications across financial services, healthcare, and retail. The author emphasizes that metadata must be treated as a strategic asset rather than an operational afterthought to overcome barriers in data discovery, contextual interpretation, and governance. The study details how metadata supports the entire AI lifecycle—from data sourcing and preparation to model training, evaluation, and deployment—and reviews architectural components like centralized data catalogs, knowledge graphs, and semantic layers for establishing robust data ecosystems.
Tags (comma separated): data discoverability, knowledge graphs, semantic interoperability

Title: How an AI-ready National Data Library would help UK science
Author/Organization: Albert Meroño-Peñuela, Joe Massey, Andrew Newman, and Elena Simperl
Summary: This paper provides a technical vision and architectural blueprint for building an AI-ready National Data Library (NDL) in the UK, designed to make government and public datasets seamlessly reusable for scientific discovery. Utilizing the Open Data Institute’s Multilayer Interoperability Framework (MIF), the authors outline a technical stack featuring standardized dataset metadata (such as DCAT and Croissant), AI-powered data quality analysis tools, evaluation benchmarks, and dashboards. Additionally, the paper highlights AI-enabled harmonization services (such as data cleaning, vocabulary mapping, synthetic data generation, and federated learning) and proposes a user-centric governance model to balance privacy, public benefit, and innovation.
Tags (comma separated): data infrastructure, standardized vocabularies, FAIR principles, data stewardship

Title: FAIR: Making Data AI-Ready
Author/Organization: Susanna-Assunta Sansone, Philippe Rocca-Serra, Mark Wilkinson, and Lee Harland
Publication: FAIR: Making Data AI-Ready (Chapter 33 of AIR_WG_2023), published in 2023 by World Scientific Publishing Company
Summary: This article explores how the FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data principles serve as a fundamental prerequisite for modern data science and machine learning applications. It emphasizes that poorly described public domain data require substantial manual preparation, creating bottlenecks for AI analytics. The authors examine technical and practical solutions—such as machine-readable metadata standards (schema.org, DCAT, RO-Crate), FAIR evaluation environments, semantic search utilizing ontologies, and industrial implementations within the biopharmaceutical sector—to make datasets natively machine-actionable and prepared for digital transformations.

Title: Automated Data Readiness for Scientific AI
Author/Organization: Sean R. Wilkinson, Valentine G. Anantharaj, Jong Youl Choi, Ketan Maheshwari, Marshall McDonnell, Massimiliano Lupo Pasini, Polina Shpilker, Renan Souza, Patrick Widener, Sarp Oral, and Wesley Brewer
Summary: This paper introduces REDI (Readiness Engine for Data Integration), an open-source framework designed to automate scientific data readiness across a unified five-stage pipeline (ingest, preprocess, transform, structure, and output). Paired with companion tool SetGo for FAIR compliance and catalog publishing, REDI aims to eliminate the manual data preparation bottleneck where researchers spend 70% to 80% of project effort cleaning data. The framework is evaluated across diverse scientific domains—including climate science, proteomics, materials science, and nuclear fusion—demonstrating successful automated transformation, near-ideal parallel scaling on high-performance computing systems, and format selection optimization.

Title: Toward AI-Ready Medical Imaging Data
Author/Organization: Milen Nikolov, Edilberto Amorim, J. Harry Caufield, Nayoon Gim, Nomi L. Harris, Jared Houghtaling, Xiang Li, Danielle Morrison, Anaïs Rameau, Jamie Shaffer, Hari Trivedi, and Monica C. Munoz-Torres
Publication: Unpublished manuscript / preprint via the NIH Bridge to Artificial Intelligence (Bridge2AI) Consortium, 2024
