Summary: This article addresses the infrastructure and standardization challenges of utilizing medical imaging data for artificial intelligence, focusing heavily on the Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine (DICOM) standard. Developed by members of the NIH Bridge2AI Standards Working Group, the guide establishes practical Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) spanning a seven-stage data lifecycle: data extraction and metadata characterization, file integrity verification, data completeness and conformance checks, metadata tag validation, image quality and pixel data validation, metadata consistency, and pixel/metadata de-identification (such as defacing MRI and CT scans to protect patient privacy).
Tags (comma separated): medical imaging, Findable Accessible Interoperable and Reusable (FAIR), De-identification (defacing), Metadata characterization

Title: Data readiness pipeline patterns for scientific AI at scale: Insights from climate, fusion, life sciences, and materials
Author/Organization: Wesley Brewer, Patrick Widener, Valentine Anantharaj, Feiyi Wang, Tom Beck, Arjun Shankar, and Sarp Oral
Publication: AI Magazine, Vol. 47, e70056, published in 2026 by John Wiley & Sons Ltd on behalf of AAAI
Summary: This article examines the application of Data Readiness for AI (DRAI) principles to massive datasets used to train scientific foundation models across climate, nuclear fusion, life sciences, and materials science. The authors introduce a two-dimensional conceptual maturity matrix combining canonical preprocessing patterns (download, ingest, preprocess, transform, structure, shard) with a five-level operational readiness scale tailored for high-performance computing (HPC) environments. Through case studies on models like ClimaX, AFLOW, OpenFold, and fusion disruption prediction workflows, the paper highlights common bottlenecks like file I/O constraints and formatting fragmentation, offering actionable recommendations for scalable AI pipeline design.
Tags (comma separated): data encoding standards, data syntax standards, knowledge graph

Title: SciHorizon: Benchmarking AI-for-Science Readiness from Scientific Data to Large Language Models
Author/Organization: Chuan Qin, Xin Chen, Chengrui Wang, Pengmin Wu, Xi Chen, Yihang Cheng, Jingyi Zhao, Meng Xiao, Xiangchao Dong, Qingqing Long, Boya Pan, Han Wu, Chengzan Li, Yuanchun Zhou, Hui Xiong, and Hengshu Zhu
Publication: Proceedings of the 31st ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (KDD ’25), August 3–7, 2025, Toronto, ON, Canada
Summary: This paper proposes SciHorizon, a comprehensive assessment framework that benchmarks AI-for-Science readiness from both data and Large Language Model (LLM) perspectives. For data, it introduces a framework comprising four primary dimensions—Quality, FAIRness, Explainability, and Compliance—and provides curated dataset recommendations across Earth, Life, and Materials Sciences based on peer-reviewed literature from 2018 to 2023. For model evaluation, SciHorizon establishes a fine-grained capability matrix spanning five core indicators (Knowledge, Understanding, Reasoning, Multimodality, and Values) across major scientific disciplines, utilizing it to benchmark over 50 representative open-source and closed-source LLMs.

Title: Architectural Evolution and Selection Framework for Database Systems in AI-Ready Data Platforms
Summary: This paper introduces a unified cross-paradigm evaluation and selection framework for database architecture design within modern AI-ready data platforms. The author argues that selecting database architectures in enterprise environments typically relies on ad-hoc engineering intuition rather than systematic guidance across heterogeneous database systems. To bridge this gap, the paper evaluates thirteen major database paradigms (spanning transactional, analytical, and AI-oriented systems) across nine architectural dimensions—such as data model, consistency, scaling strategy, storage layout, query model, workload fit, latency profile, cost model, and operational complexity. It proposes a three-stage selection framework comprising workload profiling, constraint filtering, and weighted compatibility scoring. Grounded by a financial fraud detection enterprise case study, the research identifies three major convergence and evolution patterns: the decoupling of compute and storage, workload-driven specialization, and convergence toward integrated AI-ready platforms that incorporate lakehouse storage, feature processing, and semantic retrieval layers.
Tags (comma separated): database architecture selection, database systems, distributed databases, lakehouse architecture, NoSQL, spacVector databases

Title: Data Preprocessing Techniques for AI and Machine Learning Readiness: Scoping Review of Wearable Sensor Data in Cancer Care
Author/Organization: Bengie L Ortiz, Vibhuti Gupta, Rajnish Kumar, Aditya Jalin, Xiao Cao, Charles Ziegenbein, Ashutosh Singhal, Muneesh Tewari, and Sung Won Choi
Summary: This study presents a scoping review following PRISMA-ScR guidelines to examine preprocessing techniques applied to raw wearable sensor data in cancer care, specifically focusing on ensuring data readiness for artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) applications. Out of an initial 2147 identified articles, 20 peer-reviewed studies met the inclusion criteria. The review categorized preprocessing workflows into three main areas: data transformation (found in 60% of the studies, e.g., time segmentation, feature calculation, Fourier transform), normalization and standardization (found in 40%, e.g., z-score scaling, min-max normalization), and data cleaning (found in 40%, e.g., imputation, outlier removal, artifact filtering). The authors highlight a widespread lack of standardized best practices across oncology mHealth studies and propose a generalized, adaptable data preprocessing framework to improve data reliability, reduce model bias, and streamline AI/ML applications in continuous health monitoring.
Tags (comma separated): machine learning, data preprocessing, cancer care

Title: From Raw EO Data to AI-Ready Datasets: Lowering the Barrier to Geospatial Foundation Model Fine-Tuning
Author/Organization: Mattia Santoro, Enrico Boldrini, Stefano Nativi, and Paolo Mazzetti
Summary: This article addresses the technical bottlenecks involved in preparing Earth Observation (EO) data for fine-tuning Geospatial Foundation Models (GFMs) like Prithvi-EO 2.0 and TerraMind 1.0. Recognizing that formatting, aligning spatial references, and generating inputs manually is labor-intensive, the authors introduce a fully automated, open-source Python library named EO AI Ready. The paper details a structured data model (representing datasets, splits, and geospatial coverages) and an orchestrator-pattern architecture that connects target labels with spatiotemporally aligned EO data via STAC catalogs and cloud endpoints. Benchmarking experiments across multi-temporal crop classification, land use/land cover mapping, and wildfire scar detection demonstrate that datasets generated automatically via this library achieve downstream AI performance comparable to—and in some cases slightly exceeding—those built using original, dataset-specific manual pipelines.
Tags (comma separated): geospatial foundation models; AI-ready data; machine learning; earth observation

Title: Building AI-Ready Data Systems for Space Life Sciences, Aerospace Medicine, and Deep Space Exploration
Author/Organization: Sylvain V. Costes, Sergio Garcia Busto, Ryan T. Scott, James A. Casaletto, Gautier Bardi de Fourtou, Brian M. Evarts, Amanda M. Saravia-Butler, Xavier-Lewis Palmer, Rodrigo Coutinho de Almeida, Laetitia Frost, Jelena Tešić, Afshin Beheshti, Christopher E. Mason, Peter W. Rose, Sergio E. Baranzini, Lauren M. Sanders, Stefania Giacomello, and Pedro Madrigal
Summary: This perspective article argues that while artificial intelligence holds immense potential for space life sciences and deep space exploration (such as Artemis and future crewed Mars missions), leveraging AI requires moving beyond basic FAIR data sharing toward fully standardized, machine-actionable, "AI-ready" and "space-ready" data architectures. The authors examine the challenges of small sample sizes, high data heterogeneity, and mission-specific constraints across multi-omics, telemetry, and imaging modalities. To solve these gaps, they propose a comprehensive roadmap featuring an Apache Parquet/Arrow-based data layer, AI-assisted biocuration via LinkML and OntoGPT schemas, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers for agentic routing, knowledge graph integrations (such as the SPOKE-GeneLab proxy network), and a three-zone federated learning architecture (successfully demonstrated on the International Space Station via the FLUID framework) to preserve data privacy across international agencies and commercial partners.
Tags (comma separated): space life sciences, metadata, access interfaces

Title: Laying the Foundation: Why Data Readiness is the Cornerstone of Successful AI Initiatives
Publication: Journal of Computer Science and Technology Studies
Summary: This article positions data readiness as the essential prerequisite for implementing successful and sustainable artificial intelligence initiatives across enterprises. The author argues that many AI projects fail because organizations prioritize advanced computational models while treating data preparation as an afterthought. To address this issue, the paper presents a structured data readiness framework that encompasses quality dimensions (accuracy, consistency, and reliability), completeness, contextual integrity (metadata and domain knowledge), and lineage tracking. It further examines how Master Data Management (MDM) and regulatory alignment (such as compliance with the EU AI Act) can be built directly into enterprise data architectures. By analyzing case studies in healthcare, insurance, and supply chain logistics, the article demonstrates how structured assessments and data readiness practices systematically improve operational performance and reduce downstream failures.
Tags (comma separated): data readiness, information governance, entity management, quality architecture

Title: Exploratory Visual Analysis for Increasing Data Readiness in Artificial Intelligence Projects
Author/Organization: Mattias Tiger, Daniel Jakobsson, Anders Ynnerman, Fredrik Heintz, and Daniel Jönsson
Summary: This paper bridges the gap between data-centered AI and the visualization community by demonstrating how exploratory visual analysis can be used to assess and improve data readiness. The authors expand on traditional data readiness frameworks (specifically Neil D. Lawrence’s A-B-C bands) by integrating explicit considerations for time-varying data, text, and distribution shifts. They map specific data readiness questions to targeted visualization techniques (such as using 2D projections of language model embeddings to audit text and using aggregated time plots to find temporal shifts) to identify data anomalies. Additionally, the paper concretizes "Band A" (application feasibility) by analyzing hyperparameter tuning landscapes and validation error distributions. The authors validate their visual guidelines through three real-world case studies: predicting traffic disturbances, forecasting public transit arrival/departure times, and optimizing team and task assignments.
